To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
1) Yersinia‐induced CD4 Th1 T cells from PP and/or MLN are protective against Yersinia‐infection in vivo.
intestinal CD4 T cells are involved in the defence at different sites of Yersinia entercolitica infection, and that the distribution pattern correlates with their protective properties.
(i) intestinal T cells are protective against Y. enterocalitica infection, and (ii) the protection pattern is dependent on the origin of the transferred cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the characterization of the cellular immune response in the intestinal mucosa and in the lymphoid tissues draining the intestine.
the elucidation of the mechanisms involved in the pathogenesis of Yersinia enteritis.
the characterization of protective T cells against Y. entercolitica in the intestine and other sites of infection.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transfer of Yersina‐specific Th1 T cells from PP and from MLN protected against a lethal infection with Y. enteroclitia.
PP and MLN are different sites of the immune system with different functions in the defence against intestinal infections with Y. entercolitica.
the adoptively transferred T cells from MLNs and PPs were able to protect the host from Yersinia infection by reducing bacterial loads in the MLNs, spleen and PP.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Yersinia‐infected mice have T cells in the intestine which can be transferred into other Yersinia‐challenged mice and protect them.
intestinal CD4 T cell lines from PP and MLNs are involved in the defence of mice against enteropathogenic Y. enterocolita.
intestinal CD4 T cells from PP and lymph node may be involved in protection at different sites of enteropathogenic Y. enterocoltica infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intestinal T cells are involved in the defence at different sites of Yersinia infection, and that the adoptive transfer of these cells can protect from Yersinia infection.
intestinal T cells can confer protection against Y. entercolitica infection in the gut and spleen and that the distribution pattern in vivo correlates with the protection pattern.
